newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's far-rightist Le Pen in election brawl.
newsitem.headline: France's far-rightist Le Pen in election brawl.

text.p: Jean-Marie Le Pen, fiery leader of France's far-right National Front, threw a female Socialist election candidate to the ground during a campaign brawl with protesters on Friday, a government official said.

The burly 68-year-old former paratrooper got into a shoving match while campaigning for his daughter Marie Caroline Le Pen in the poor, heavily-immigrant troubled outer Paris suburb of Mantes-La-Jolie for Sunday's parliamentary election runoff.
Two people, including Socialist candidate Anette Peulvast-Bergeal, were slightly hurt, a spokesman for the local prefect (government representative) said.
"Mr Le Pen got out, caught the first person at hand who was being pushed by the crowd -- Mrs Peulvast. He seized her by her blouse and threw her to the ground," the spokesman said.
Television showed Le Pen pinning Peulvast against the wall.
Le Pen, in a statement, called the spokesman's comment "slanderous" and said he was suing him for slander.

He earlier acknowledged he had "slightly pushed" individuals he said tried to prevent him from "walking freely", but he denied throwing any punches. "When I'm attacked, I've never been afraid of another man or even several at once," he said.
During the incident, anti-racist militants hurled insults, eggs and stones at Le Pen, who was shielded from injury by a ring of police officers and private bodyguards.
The National Front accused Peulvast of heading "leftist bullies" and said Le Pen's daughter would launch legal action for violence and hampering her election campaigning.
Le Pen sees himself as kingmaker in the poll, but it could also spell the beginning of the end of his leadership.

Under his brash direction, the xenophobic party won 14.94 percent in last Sunday's first round, its best yet in a National Assembly election. Analysts say its voters will play a crucial role in the outcome of Sunday's runoff.
But a new generation of National Front leaders is seeking seats in parliament, and their success could soon eclipse the 68-year-old Le Pen in national prominence.
Pollsters predict the party will win at least one seat and perhaps as many as three in the assembly, where it now has none.
Among those angling for seats are Le Pen deputies Bruno Megret and Bruno Gollnisch, who have made no secret of their eagerness to succeed Le Pen should he step down as party chief.
Le Pen on Thursday handed out endorsements to non-Front candidates he deemed worthy of support and black marks to those he called enemies of his movement.
His behaviour showed both why he has been so successful in keeping the party in the public eye and why he remains a pariah in mainstream political circles.
At one point, a beaming Le Pen paraded around the stage carrying an oversized photograph of the head of Strasbourg mayor Catherine Trautmann, perched on a huge platter.
"I offer the head of Madame Trautmann to Marie-France Stirbois," he said, bowing to the National Front candidate in Dreux, west of Paris.
"I find that absolutely shocking," Socialist Leader Lionel Jospin said of the incident. The Socialist Trautmann had led an anti-Front mass march in her eastern city in March.

Le Pen also urged defeat for Gaullist Prime Minister Alain Juppe, Paris mayor Jean Tiberi and Justice Minister Jacques Toubon, centrist Culture Minister Philippe Douste-Blazy and Communist Party leader Robert Hue.

He called Juppe "the archetype of the most unjust and ferocious enemy of the National Front". Juppe, who last year called le Pen "deeply, almost viscerally racist, antisemitic and xenophobic", is to step down as premier after the runoff.

Le Pen's 21 recommendations were a climbdown from earlier calls to "zap the right" by voting for leftist candidates in the second round. Other Front leaders had protested that the party rank and file were bitterly opposed to the left.

Le Pen has boasted that the Front will play a decisive role in the election by only supporting candidates who endorse its anti-European stance and plan to reserve jobs, education, health care, housing and welfare for native-born French citizens.
But pollsters say his endorsements will have scant impact.
The Front will itself have candidates in 132 of France's 577 constituencies in the second round, a sign that the Front is now a major force in all French elections, analysts say.
